issues.issue: The clause equates masculine terms with all employees, but the operative text elsewhere uses "men" as a substantive category (e.g. 4-A.3 "No man may hold a regular situation", Group 4 "Casuals—Men"). Whether this preamble merely neutralizes gendered wording or reaches those defined categories is unstated.
The Agreement is made binding on each Publisher "or its successor" without defining what constitutes a successor or what obligations pass. Nothing in the instrument supplies the test.

The Metropolitan Area is fixed by "a radius of approximately fifty miles" and a line "bounded approximately as follows," leaving the outer boundary indeterminate. Whole obligations turn on it (2-E.1, 3-E, 9-A, 21-D.V "territorial coverage").

Recognition is tied to an enumerated list of operations, inviting an expressio unius reading that unlisted delivery-room work is outside the unit. The "Collectors, except ... billing system operated through the auditing department" carve-out compounds which collections are covered.

The exception for "a hospital, club comprising one building, school or other government or municipal building" ends in a general term after specific examples, leaving unclear which premises get single drop-off treatment. "Current practice in the territory" for collections and returns is likewise unfixed.

Coverage of "any other operation" depends on work "now being performed exclusively" by unit employees, and neither "now" (as of which agreement) nor "exclusively" is defined. The catch-all sits against the closed list in 2-A.1.

"New mechanical devices ... introduced to perform or aid in the performance of" unit operations has no boundary — a device that merely aids may or may not fall within it. The line against automated systems governed by 3-D.4 is not drawn.

Only terminals "located within the City of New York" are recognized as delivery points, inviting the argument that terminals elsewhere in the Metropolitan Area are excluded. The provision does not say whether the list is exhaustive.

Canada points may be established for areas "where for any reason distribution is interrupted," a trigger with no duration, cause or verification requirement. Nothing says when the point must be discontinued.

The ban on substituting buses, ferries or airplanes for "existing means or methods of delivery" is immediately qualified by a proviso preserving the right "to make substitution for a bus or railroad now being used," and the two sentences pull against each other. "Existing" and "now" are also fixed to no stated date.

Drivers are to be selected by seniority "in accordance with Section 4-B," but 4-B governs the filling of vacant or newly created regular situations, not the assignment of tractor-trailer work. The cross-reference cannot be applied as written.
"A reasonable number of employees" must be given training, with no benchmark, ratio or mechanism for fixing the number. Nothing else in the article supplies one.

The Publisher's reserved right to "continue and expand" the volume of work handed to an over-the-road carrier at the city line is hard to square with the Publishers' letter "Clarification of Method and Extent," which acknowledges that the contract prohibits subcontracting of bargaining-unit deliveries. Which governs an expansion of carrier work is unresolved.

Transfer points must lie "within the Metropolitan Area," but 22-D Point Two (iii) and (iv) direct The Times to select transfer points 150 to 250 miles from Columbus Circle, far outside that area. The two cannot both be given effect without deciding how far 22-D displaces 2-E.2(e).

Through-driving to "Albany or any other city designated by the Publisher" conflicts with 22-D Point Two(i), which excepts common-carrier runs beyond 250 miles or with more than two stops from unit driving. Which controls a long designated run is unstated.
Combination runs turn on "presently recognized exchange points at or near the city line," a set never identified anywhere in the Agreement. There is no mechanism for fixing or changing them.

The Publishers may unilaterally discontinue runs on a "jurisdictional dispute with another union," which is difficult to reconcile with 16-M.3's rule that no change in condition may be put into effect without the other party's prior consent. Neither provision says which prevails.

The right to increase, decrease or discontinue over-the-road trucking "to the extent that such forms of transportation may now be employed" is expressly narrowed for The Times by 22-D Point Two(x), which forbids assigning to a common carrier a run in operation nine consecutive months. The scope of paragraph (h) therefore differs by Publisher without the text saying so.

The no-layoff protection applies only where the layoff is "solely as a result of" establishing the run, a causation word with no test, and 3-D.1 preserves layoffs for economic or business reasons generally. Which characterization applies to a layoff following a new trailer run is left open.

The requirement that home-delivery bundles be tied by unit employees is qualified by "present practice, however, excepted," an unidentified body of practice that may swallow the rule. Neither the practice nor its date is fixed.

The Union's obligation to arbitrate jurisdictional conflicts is conditioned on "such other union or unions agree[ing] to such an arbitration," so the duty may never mature and no alternative is provided. "Conditions and methods of operation now prevailing" is likewise undated.

Union jurisdiction attaches "when full operations commence" at an annex or new building, and "full operations" is nowhere defined or measured. Partial or phased start-ups fall outside any stated rule.

Protection turns on an employee "performing satisfactorily the particular work assigned to him," with no standard for satisfactory performance. 4-A.4's "qualified and competent" requirement uses a different formulation for the same subject.

The first sentence is mutilated — "Any employee shall be entitled to for work in the performance of the several operations set forth in this section of the office or plant" — omitting the verb (apparently "to shape") that carries the right. What entitlement is created cannot be read off the words.

The clause promises maximum union security "to the extent embodied in Section 17 of this agreement," but 17-A.1 states that the union-security language printed there is "for reference only and not as a part of this Agreement." The reference therefore points to text the contract disclaims.

The sixth-shift overtime sentence reproduces, nearly word for word, part of the italicized former "2-L" set out in 17-A.1 as not part of this Agreement. Two provisions bearing the same section designation, one operative and one disclaimed, cannot be read together without construction.

The flat bar on an employee engaging "any person to aid him in the performance of the work assigned to him" sits against Section 10-B, which defines a half-day boy as working "in aid of and under the direction of a route man." Whether the routeman's use of a half-day boy is excepted is not stated.

Deductions are fixed to "the second pay check of the employee in each month," while the October 26, 1981 Weekly Checkoff letter obliges the Publisher to amend 2-N.1 for weekly or bi-weekly checkoff on sixty days' notice. The two prescribe different mechanics for the same deduction.

The agency fee is "a flat amount payable for each shift worked" but capped so that "the amount payable per shift" not exceed 5% of monthly dues, mixing per-shift and monthly measures. Whether the cap is per shift or on the aggregate is not resolved by the words.

The Publisher must continue "the schedules shown in the last notice of such schedules to the Union," an unidentified document with no date or copy incorporated. Which notice controls is left to proof outside the instrument.

This leaves "the conditions under which tailmen are to be employed" to each Publisher's published schedule, while 21-C.3(g) and the 21-D schedules fix tailman thresholds for The News by number of loads. Which source governs tailman manning is not stated.

The Union's right of complaint turns on schedules being "unduly burdensome," and the Publisher's on "newspaper operational conditions warrant[ing]" a change; neither phrase has a defined content. Nothing in Section 16 supplies a standard.

The Publisher's right to fix "the number of dealers to be served on the several respective routes" cannot be squared with 21-D.I.A, which caps maximum dealers per route by papers per load at Newspoint. Which prevails on a News direct-delivery route is unaddressed.

The recognized right to lay off and rearrange routes "as such Publisher may find necessary or desirable" runs against 3-D.4, which forbids layoff of listed situation holders because of automation. Whether a rearrangement following an automated installation is reviewable as economic is the fault line.

The definition is circular — "economic or business reasons" mean "all reasons of an economic or business character" in their "usual and ordinary sense" — and expressly disclaims prior practice as a guide. It supplies no boundary for the term it defines.

The duty to "give employment to those regular situation holders laid off by the wholesaler or news company" cannot be squared with the hiring order and Adjustment Board lists of 4-A.2, which control who is hired and in what sequence. Where such transferees fit in the Groups is unstated.

The protected list is of situation holders "as of May 1, 1981" but the protection runs against automation installed "after May 1, 1965," a sixteen-year mismatch that the text never explains. Which date governs the protection is on the face of the clause unclear.

Everything turns on "a determination duly made" that automation created an excess of regular situations, yet the clause never says who makes it or by what procedure. The two-week deadline runs from an event no one is assigned to declare.

This preserves the Publisher's obligation under 5-G to maintain "as many regular situations as possible" while simultaneously subjecting it to 3-D.1's layoff right. The savings language leaves the two duties to be reconciled without a rule of priority.

Existing methods and extent of direct and combined delivery "are to be continued" with no change absent Board approval, while 3-F leaves the Publisher "free" to choose and change delivery form on new sections or routes. Whether a route is "new" therefore decides which regime applies, and neither provision defines it.
"New sections or new routes" is undefined, so a rearranged or combined existing route may be recast as new and taken out of 3-E's freeze. The clause supplies no test for novelty.

This paragraph is reproduced verbatim as 12-C in the wholesalers section, so the same subject is governed twice in different places. A court asked whether one qualifies or supersedes the other has nothing in the text to go on.

The safety duties are stated as "undue hardship or hazard," "excessive work tasks" and protection "insofar as practicable," none of which has a defined measure. The provision then routes non-compliance complaints to the Board without supplying a standard for it to apply.

The insurance amount reads "$20,000, $50,000 beginning January 1, 1982," leaving both the initial figure and the mechanics of the increase uncertain on the face of the clause. The 1987 Memorandum's reference to raising this coverage "from $60,000" does not match either printed number.

The parties must make "every effort" to eliminate advance-section overtime "in so far as that may be practicable," and the same sentence then disclaims any obligation to do so. The duty created is not measurable.

The Publisher may purchase employee-owned equipment "at its then fair value," with no valuation method or appraiser named. Termination of existing arrangements when equipment "no longer is fit for use" is equally unmeasured.

The first sentence lets advertising and promotional matter be "handled, distributed or disposed of as the Publisher may direct," while the second requires that a defined class of such matter "be tied, handled and delivered by an extra crew." The two directions conflict as to matter falling in both descriptions.

The most-favored-terms duty reaches contracts with "any person publishing within the City of New York," a narrower geography than the Metropolitan Area used throughout the Agreement. Publishers just outside the city line fall into a gap the clause never addresses.

The Union must use its "best efforts collectively and individually to promote the business and interests of the several Publishers," a duty with no benchmark and no stated content. Nothing in the Agreement says what performance satisfies it.

The enumerated "immediate family" includes "grandmother, grandfather" without saying whose — the employee's, the spouse's, or both — a point The Times had to clarify by side letter in 1988 precisely because the terms "have not always been interpreted and applied consistently." The list also mixes named relations with "legal dependents as defined by the Internal Revenue Code."

Foremen and assistant foremen are placed on the seniority and priority lists here, while 6-B makes their hours, wages and conditions "a matter of agreement between the Publisher and such foreman" with a right of removal at will. Whether a foreman carries seniority for layoff cannot be answered from either alone.

Seniority is given two meanings — length of service in the regular-situation capacity in (a) and "length of service based on regularity and continuity of service" in (b) — introduced only by the word "Otherwise." Which measure governs a given dispute is left to construction.

Group 1 listing may be approved for loss of a situation "because of illness, physical incapacity or for other such good and sufficient cause," a catch-all following two specific medical grounds. Whether the general words are confined to causes of that kind is the classic ejusdem generis question.

Group 3 status is given to "men who signify their intention to and do shape steadily," and "steadily" is defined nowhere. The shape requirements in 4-A.2(e) state a different, numeric test for retention.

Casuals are "men who are not connected with the industry," while "industry" is defined in 4-A.2(i) by reference to employing companies, not to individuals' connections. Who counts as unconnected is therefore untested.

Promotion to vacant regular situations is ordered from Group 1 then Group 3, omitting Group 2 industry extras entirely, while 4-B says such situations are "filled permanently ... from among the regular situation holders" by seniority. The temporary/permanent split leaves the two rules in tension.

Retention requires shaping six shifts "per week or work[ing] five (5) shifts per week," but credit is limited to one shift per twenty-four hours and only if present at hiring, so the two requirements may not both be satisfiable in a week. The interaction of the shape count and the credit rule is not worked out.

A foreman needing more men than the list holds "may engage such men as he may be able to obtain," which is difficult to square with the same paragraph's rule that only the Adjustment Board may add to or change the lists and with the hiring order of 4-A.2(b). The status of men so engaged is unaddressed.

The definition of "industry" is ungrammatical — "all companies employing persons engaged in the categories contained in Section 2 hereof by any Publisher, newspaper distributor or wholesaler" — so it is unclear whether the companies or the categories are being qualified. Group 2 seniority and Group 1 transfer rights turn on this word.

The 2% cap is measured against "the total number of situations in the delivery room of said Publisher," a unit of count that no provision defines for multi-plant publishers. 6-D contemplates more than one plant per Publisher.
The fractions are printed as "one third (4)" and "two thirds (34)," so the numerals contradict the words. The annual transfer allocation cannot be computed from the text as printed.

"Qualified and competent for the work or the job in question" states the hiring and promotion bar without any definition or objective measure of competence. 4-H sends such questions to the Board without supplying a standard.

The vacancy is to be filled permanently "from among the regular situation holders in accord with their seniority standing," while 4-A.1(b) says promotional priority — not seniority — determines who may claim a newly created or vacant regular situation. The two selection rules cannot both govern.

An unemployed (Group 1) extra who refuses a situation is "placed at the top of the Group 3 regular extra list" while a Group 3 extra who refuses goes to the end, so refusal moves the senior man into a junior group at a favorable position. Whether that is a penalty or a benefit is not resolvable from the words.

The exceptions apply only "provided notice in writing has been given to the Publisher," with no time limit stated for that notice and no consequence specified for late notice. Whether a belated writing preserves the situation is unaddressed.

Consent to a leave of absence "shall not be unreasonably withheld," a standard the Agreement nowhere elaborates, and the same test is applied again to extensions. There is no stated maximum duration for such leaves.

Paragraph (a) deems the situation vacated once the absence periods are reached, while (c) makes vacancy depend on a certified letter and the absence of an explanation within thirty days. Whether the situation is vacated automatically or only after the letter procedure is the conflict.

Restoration is given to employees "absent for the foregoing reasons," which may refer to the four enumerated reasons in 4-F.1(a) or to any absence covered by the whole of 4-F including (c). The antecedent is not fixed.

The day shift is defined as falling "between the period of 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m." while 5-B defines the night shift as between 6:00 p.m. and 10:00 a.m., so the two periods overlap by hours at both ends. Which rate and which shift rules govern work in the overlap is not stated.

The night-shift window of 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 a.m. overlaps the 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. day-shift window fixed by 5-A, and the Agreement pays different rates for each. Nothing designates which classification controls work performed in the overlapping hours.

The day work week is printed as "no more than 8915 hours per week," a figure that is not a number of hours and cannot be reconciled with the 7 hours 54 minutes day fixed by 5-A. The weekly ceiling cannot be read off the text.

The obligation to stagger the work week "so that as many regular situations as possible may be created and maintained" states a maximizing duty with no measure of what is possible. 3-D.6 makes this same undefined obligation the anchor of the automation protections.
